title: E56 - AI-Pilled, Not AI-First: Arlo Devlin-Brown, Founding Principal, TDB Law
author: Arlo Devlin-Brown

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions

This is compatible with the cluster’s copilot framing, but it does not assess Harvey’s prestige-led strategy, commercial traction, workflow-infrastructure ambitions, governance, or defensibility, and explicitly declines to evaluate the current product.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source accepts that practical legal-AI value comes from context-rich, tailored workflows rather than isolated prompts, and extends this specifically to litigation through continuously updated, case-aware agents and hands-on workflow discovery. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that current adoption remains basic and that larger agentic gains are prospective rather than measured.

st.an: Devlin-Brown accepts that AI will reduce associate leverage and reshape the law-firm pyramid, while materially extending the cluster with a concrete alternative: smaller teams in which partners work directly with juniors and AI absorbs tedious tasks. He therefore treats the training effect as a potential improvement to apprenticeship, while acknowledging that junior lawyers initially lack the judgment needed to assess AI-assisted work.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s value will depend on organisational adaptation and resulting changes to service delivery, rather than access to the technology alone. It materially extends the cluster by identifying in-house capability, pressure on low-value external work, client AI literacy and defensible vendor selection as specific commercial mechanisms, while treating effects on firms and billing as forecasts rather than measured outcomes.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Devlin-Brown accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it with a concrete case-embedded agent workflow for litigation. He also develops the verification point by calibrating review intensity to consequence: preliminary orientation can tolerate immaterial imperfections, while court filings require exacting verification. His emphasis on experienced judgment, training and law-firm adaptation further reinforces work redesign rather than wholesale lawyer replacement.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s emphasis on strengthening established legal expertise through intelligent AI use rather than treating AI-native identity or autonomous substitution as the goal. Its recommendations are normative and experiential, not evidence of demonstrated transformation or customer outcomes.

st.an: The source supports the proposition that corporate legal departments are positioned to capture AI gains and pressure outside providers because AI offers faster, cheaper internal answers while in-house cost incentives conflict with BigLaw’s leverage model. Its substitution evidence is anecdotal rather than systematic and does not establish market-wide insourcing or savings.

st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s conditional, user-centred optimism: it recommends using AI to strengthen established professional expertise while rejecting AI-native branding as a necessary identity. It predicts that corporate legal departments will internalise more work and resist high prices for marginal outside-counsel improvements, while also agreeing that leading firms and hourly billing can remain resilient through adaptation. st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Devlin-Brown supports the cluster’s lawyer-guided augmentation framing: AI can enable a smaller, more efficient practice, but professional experience and legal judgment—not AI adoption or an AI-native identity—remain the basis of client value. The source offers personal assessment rather than measured evidence or a material extension of the proposition.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Devlin-Brown supports the synthesis’s broader claim that AI will change legal delivery, buyer expectations and competition without producing uniform replacement. He particularly reinforces the shift toward stronger in-house capability and matter-specific, context-retaining AI workflows, while expecting continued demand for excellent outside firms and hourly billing. His account is experiential and predictive rather than evidence of repeatable-service economics or firm-wide transformation.

st.an: The source supports selective augmentation by presenting AI as a way to accelerate automatable or preparatory work so lawyers can devote more attention to case analysis, creativity and litigation strategy. st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Devlin-Brown directly supports the proposition that AI will restructure legal-service production rather than eliminate lawyers: he predicts lower associate leverage, smaller teams, buyer-side pricing pressure and continued demand for excellent firms and experienced judgment. His claims are chiefly practice-based predictions and anecdotes, not measured evidence of market-wide productivity or displacement.

kp.k: AI literacy requires experimentation, not merely chatbot adoption
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz distinguishes using AI for discrete tasks from developing instincts about its possibilities, limitations and future development. Against an unnamed partner's claim that this mindset cannot be taught, he argues it can be developed. Devlin-Brown similarly recommends repeated practical use to develop judgment about outputs; these are practitioner recommendations rather than measured training findings.
qs: Being AI-pilled means developing a foundational understanding of AI.
An AI-pilled attorney isn't just using AI in order to accomplish a task. They're using AI in order to better understand AI.
But the only way you develop the feel for that sort of thing is just to do it. To do it a lot.

kp.k: Smaller teams could replace high associate leverage
kp.d: Devlin-Brown predicts declining need for high associate-to-partner ratios. Recalling investigations involving teams of 20 or more people, sometimes supplemented by contract document reviewers, he estimates that five good associates could now handle those matters, with many cases requiring only one or two. These are retrospective practitioner estimates, not measured staffing reductions. He argues smaller teams enable direct partner involvement and closer mentorship.
qs: We don't have the seven associates per partner ratio.
whatever you do with AI, there's not going to be a need for that kind of leverage anymore.
we had teams of, of 20 or more people and maybe some outside contract lawyers reviewing documents.
But that same case, you could, you could have done each of those with five good associates.
And when you can do it that way, you get to work with everyone directly and know what they're doing.

kp.k: Junior development shifts toward mentorship and tool building
kp.d: Abramowitz characterizes TDB's recruitment approach as a teaching-hospital model rather than eliminating juniors, reporting Pearson Ferdinand's public position that it does not hire junior associates. Devlin-Brown wants juniors who experiment and build with AI rather than merely execute a partner's prompts. Both argue that smaller teams and reduced tedious work can improve formation, while Devlin-Brown cautions that automating chronologies does not remove the obligation to learn the documents and case.
qs: the model is switching from leverage to true mentorship and true almost like teaching hospital format
You need to, to learn how to play with this stuff and build with it so that you can be better than the partner and add some value, add some value there.
You're still going to have to, they're still going to have to learn to learn the case.
But by having the less leverage teams, partners are going to get to work with them more directly.

kp.k: Experience can advantage senior lawyers in AI use
kp.d: The speakers dispute the assumption that younger lawyers necessarily lead adoption. Devlin-Brown describes recent graduates receiving conflicting messages: AI as cheating, professional risk and a threat to their jobs, without adequate training. He argues experienced lawyers can apply accumulated judgment to AI-generated work in ways beginners cannot immediately replicate. Abramowitz recommends using AI to understand legal purposes and strategies rather than simply delegating drafting.
qs: And then it's a thing of like, you better not do this because it's cheating.
And then they're bombarded with, you know, like, but by the way, this is going to replace all your jobs.

the best thing that you can do if you're a junior attorney is learn about what it takes to be an attorney

kp.k: Embedded agents organize matters and coordinate legal research
kp.d: Devlin-Brown describes his own workflow, which shifted after more agentic capabilities arrived at the beginning of 2026. He primarily uses Claude co-work, also uses Claude code, and maintains case descriptions, workstreams, update protocols and markdown records to compensate for limited project memory. Agents scan email, index discovery and coordinate research through Westlaw, mid page and court listener. He retains substantive review, including reading affidavits and promising cases himself. This is a reported individual practice, not a comparative performance evaluation.
qs: I have Claude co-work open all the time when I'm going to a case, I switch over to the project.
It creates various work streams. It has protocols for updating all of that as they go forward.
go have Westlaw run a deep research report on this situation.
And then I'll read the case, right?
So it's sort of become like the operating system. And and a sort of shared project memory.

kp.k: Persistent agents still struggle with time and stale facts
kp.d: Devlin-Brown reports that agents can remain attached to outdated case information: in his example, an earlier $30,000 claim conflicts with a later 60,000 figure. His response is to integrate Outlook email scans into case-specific routines, daily or weekly depending on the matter, and save communications in markdown for the agent. He presents this as an iteratively developed workaround, not a complete solution to memory or temporal reasoning.
qs: they're not so great with time.
The 30 is three weeks ago.
Just do a scan every, you know, day or week, depending on the case.
Look for the emails, pull them down in a markdown format.

kp.k: Workflow integration may matter more than standalone platforms
kp.d: Devlin-Brown favors assistants embedded where matter files already reside, ideally within a secure enterprise environment, over uploading documents into a separate platform. He considers expense and flexibility disadvantages of Harvey for his small firm, but explicitly limits his assessment to an earlier demo and disclaims knowledge of current Harvey or Lagora capabilities. His expectation that embedded assistants will prove more attractive to large firms is a prediction.
qs: I'm not really in a position to judge what it's like today, because I haven't haven't seen it myself.
I think the mark up and the expense on it is is very significant.
I think the the lack of flexibility is an issue.
they are not going to want to upload all of their stuff to some other platform and then start doing things in that platform.
integrate a really smart assistant into the matter files that already exists.

kp.k: Big-law marketing can outrun substantive AI adoption
kp.d: Devlin-Brown contrasts skepticism around his 2025 departure from big law with more public adoption commitments roughly a year later, which he partly attributes to corporate-client pressure. Based on conversations with former colleagues, he believes actual usage remains uneven and below marketing claims. His example of a partner becoming his firm's top Harvey user through basic applications is anecdotal evidence, not a representative adoption survey.
qs: I think probably to a significant degree under pressure from corporate clients are now like consistently saying they're adopting AI
I don't think the adoption is anything like what what the marketing is.
just basic stuff, but he's a top user.

kp.k: Exploration and final legal submissions require different verification
kp.d: Devlin-Brown distinguishes preliminary orientation and creative hypothesis testing from important decisions and court filings, where citations must be fully correct. He says AI lowers the cost of exploring arguments and factual theories that would previously have gone unexamined. His confidence that general-topic explanations are usually correct is his assessment, not a measured accuracy finding. The workflow remains lawyer-supervised: exploration generates leads for later substantive checking.
qs: If the decision is important, if it's a brief being filed in court, every pin site needs to be 100% correct.

But I never would have run them down before.
And you don't care in that scenario if everything is exactly right, because you're exploring.

kp.k: Hallucination responses should distinguish severity and substantive consequences
kp.d: Devlin-Brown argues that incorrect pinpoint citations or small quotation alterations supporting undisputed propositions differ materially from invented cases supporting nonexistent law. He still calls minor errors sloppy and says work should be checked. Abramowitz conjectures that problematic AI-assisted briefs may be outnumbered by unproblematic ones by roughly a thousand to one or more, and proposes studying pre- and post-ChatGPT briefs; neither claim is supported by a study in this transcript. Devlin-Brown distinguishes historical boilerplate errors from fabricated cases.
qs: people need to stop treating all hallucinations as the same thing.
It's still sloppy. But that is so different than lawyers who are submitting totally fake made up cases with fictitious quotes supporting invented points of law that do not exist

kp.k: AI improves preliminary client preparation and boutique range
kp.d: Abramowitz reports seeing AI-adept lawyers arrive at prospective-client meetings ready to discuss case theory rather than primarily promote team credentials. Devlin-Brown agrees and says boutiques can rapidly acquire preliminary understanding of adjacent specialties, using a bankruptcy adversary proceeding within a white-collar matter as his example. He qualifies this as preparation for assessing capability and discussing a case, not a substitute for further work after engagement.

kp.k: Litigation benefits extend beyond document summarization
kp.d: Abramowitz suggests that creative and strategic applications may make AI especially valuable for litigators in 2026; this is his comparative framing, not an established finding. Devlin-Brown stresses litigation's unpredictable, adversarial character and the value of flexible triage and idea generation. He nevertheless describes current litigator adoption as limited, with basic summarization and inconsistency detection more common than persistent agents that already know the case.

kp.k: In-house AI changes outside counsel's value proposition
kp.d: Devlin-Brown predicts profound corporate legal-department adoption because reducing external spend or internalizing work serves their cost-center incentives. AI gives buyers an independent baseline for speed, cost and acceptable quality, challenging fees justified by large teams. His $100,000 memo that is only 4% better than an internally generated answer is illustrative, not measured. He recounts a GC recreating prior advice and a PowerPoint with AI while waiting four or five days for a firm to retrieve it; this is an anecdote about substitution and responsiveness.

kp.k: Corporate leadership creates incentives for legal AI literacy
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that executive awareness, pressure for visible AI successes, access to workplace chatbots and fewer conflicting client policies can favor in-house adoption. He reports Wordsmith CEO Ross McNair's account of referrals arising when CEOs praised legal departments' AI integration, and cites an ACC CLO survey from earlier in 2026 identifying AI literacy as the professional skill CLOs believe CEOs most want them to learn; no sample or methodology is supplied. Devlin-Brown separately reports GCs seeking literacy discussions because of internal pressure.

they want to learn about it and, and learn more literacy because they're getting that pressure within their, their in-house legal departments.

kp.k: Large firms may adapt rather than disappear
kp.d: Devlin-Brown anticipates substantial reshuffling between firms as adaptation differs, but rejects the idea that AI eliminates demand for top-tier firms. He expects AI to increase business complexity and sustain demand for sophisticated advice, while enabling more lawyers to serve previously underserved market segments. That market-expansion claim is general, not specific evidence about unmet civil legal need. He does not predict the end of hourly billing; Abramowitz suggests hourly rates should rise, and Devlin-Brown agrees.
qs: there will be a lot of shuffling, a lot of changes
there's going to be a real need for excellent law firms. And that's not going anywhere. It's just a question of adapting.
I think you're going to get a lot more lawyers servicing areas of the market that we're never served.
I'm not going to say hourly billing is going to go away.

kp.d: Devlin-Brown interprets large-firm purchases of Harvey and Lagora partly as ways to demonstrate AI adoption to clients and provide reputational insulation if something goes wrong. He predicts a major AI-related breach but explicitly says he has not seen such an incident. This is speculation about procurement incentives and future risk, not evidence that either vendor has suffered a breach or that purchasing their products establishes legal compliance.

kp.k: Professional expertise remains central to the firm's identity
kp.d: Devlin-Brown resists branding TDB as AI-first or AI-native because he wants clients to hire the firm for experienced legal judgment and quality rather than tool use. He presents AI as enabling greater efficiency and sophisticated practice on a smaller platform. He endorses Abramowitz's formulation that capable lawyers should use AI intelligently to become better lawyers without making AI the firm's defining proposition.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Arlo Devlin-Brown predicts that AI will reduce associate-to-partner leverage and enable smaller litigation teams with more direct mentorship.
pts.d: Drawing on his experience supervising large investigations, Devlin-Brown says matters previously staffed with 20 or more people could have been handled with five good associates using AI; many matters could use one or two. These are retrospective estimates, not reported results of a controlled comparison. He argues that smaller teams let partners see juniors' work directly and delegate tedious tasks to AI. He does not advocate eliminating junior lawyers: juniors should learn to build with AI and contribute more than executing partners' prompts. Automating chronologies does not remove the need to understand underlying documents and learn the case.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown describes embedded matter-level AI agents as a working assistant and shared project memory, and predicts advantages over separate upload-based platforms.
pts.d: He reports using Claude Cowork to maintain case descriptions, work streams, discovery indexes and email-derived updates, and to initiate research through Westlaw and other services. He still reads important affidavits and cases himself. His prediction is that lawyers will prefer assistants integrated into existing matter files because uploading material into another platform creates workflow friction. He regards Harvey's cost and flexibility as unattractive for his small firm, but explicitly does not claim current firsthand knowledge of Harvey or certainty about either Harvey's or Legora's integration plans. His current workflow has limitations, including restricted project memory and difficulty distinguishing superseded facts from current ones; he uses structured updates to address these problems.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown says large-firm AI purchasing and public adoption claims have advanced faster than actual use.
pts.d: He contrasts widespread skepticism around his 2025 departure from BigLaw with firms' subsequent announcements and purchases of Harvey and Legora, which he attributes partly to corporate-client pressure. He describes internal adoption as uneven and below the level suggested by marketing. His evidence consists of conversations with former colleagues and an anecdote about a senior partner who was a leading Harvey user despite using it for relatively basic tasks. He similarly describes litigators' adoption as largely limited to summarization and transcript analysis, with case-embedded agents still uncommon.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown argues that experienced lawyers can exploit AI in ways newly qualified lawyers cannot immediately replicate.
pts.d: He attributes this difference to professional judgment developed through repeated legal work, rather than age-based technological aptitude. He says recent graduates face conflicting signals: AI was initially treated as cheating or a liability, then presented as a threat to their jobs, without adequate training. His advice is to gain practical experience with the tools; he offers no easy solution to the junior-training problem. This qualifies his positive account of AI-supported mentorship: AI access alone does not confer the judgment needed to assess its work.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown says AI gives boutiques faster preparation and access to introductory knowledge outside their core specialty.
pts.d: He contrasts previously asking a specialist partner for an explanation of an adjacent field with obtaining a rapid AI overview and reviewing matter documents. His example is a white-collar investigation involving bankruptcy and an adversary proceeding. He says this can help a boutique assess whether to take a matter and discuss it persuasively with the client. He expressly distinguishes initial preparation from the additional work required after accepting the case.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown says AI makes litigation exploration cheaper and more expansive, while final legal work still requires rigorous human verification.
pts.d: He describes using AI to test arguments and factual theories that would otherwise be too time-consuming to pursue. Unproductive suggestions may lead to useful further ideas. He argues that exhaustive accuracy is not necessary at every exploratory stage, but important decisions and court submissions require complete accuracy to the best of counsel's ability. He also argues against treating minor citation or quotation errors as equivalent to fabricated authorities supporting nonexistent law. His illustration is an unnamed firm's correction of what he describes as minor errors on undisputed propositions. He does not supply measured hallucination rates or establish that AI-assisted briefs are generally more accurate.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown predicts substantial reshuffling among large firms, not the disappearance of demand for elite legal services.
pts.d: He expects firms to adapt with differing success. He argues that AI will also accelerate and complicate business activity, sustaining demand for excellent firms to address complex problems. Separately, he predicts more lawyers serving previously unserved markets. He does not identify those markets as unmet civil legal need, quantify additional demand, or specify a timetable. His claim therefore supports a broad market-expansion prediction, not a demonstrated access-to-justice outcome.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown predicts that in-house AI adoption will force outside firms to justify their incremental value rather than their staffing volume.
pts.d: He says corporate legal departments can now perform more work internally and use their own AI output as a baseline for assessing outside advice, cost and turnaround. His $100,000 memo that is only 4% better than an internal AI result is an illustrative hypothetical, not a measured comparison. He recounts a GC recreating earlier advice and a presentation with AI while waiting several days for a firm to retrieve its original work. He argues that cost-reduction incentives in-house run counter to the traditional law-firm leverage model. He does not predict that hourly billing necessarily disappears and suggests hourly rates could rise.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown interprets purchases of prominent legal-AI products as client signaling and reputational protection, and predicts an eventual major AI-related breach.
pts.d: He suggests that buying Harvey or Legora lets large firms demonstrate adoption and gives them a defensible procurement narrative if an AI-related incident occurs. This is his interpretation of market incentives, not evidence that a vendor prevents breaches or transfers legal responsibility. His breach prediction is explicitly prospective: he says he has not seen such an AI incident, contrasting it with existing law-firm cyber breaches.

pts.k: Devlin-Brown presents AI as enabling experienced lawyers to deliver work efficiently on a smaller platform, not as his firm's principal selling point.
pts.d: He rejects describing TDB as 'AI-first' because he believes clients hire its lawyers for their experience and quality. AI supports that expertise and permits efficient delivery through a boutique. He distinguishes this position from possible uses in commoditized work. He says client interest varies: some primarily want excellent work at low cost, while others actively seek AI literacy and discussion.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The interview's substantive evidence is practitioner experience, workflow descriptions and informal anecdotes rather than systematic measurement.
pts.d: Devlin-Brown draws on his prosecutorial and large-firm career, his boutique's current AI use, conversations with lawyers and GCs, and an unnamed firm's corrected filing. Team-size reductions are counterfactual estimates; market restructuring, preferred software architecture and an eventual breach are predictions. No controlled productivity studies, benchmarks, adoption survey results or quantified error-rate evidence are supplied by him. The host's speculative ratio of problematic to unproblematic briefs, proposed historical comparison of briefs, autonomous-driving analogy and reported CLO survey are not treated here as Devlin-Brown's evidence or findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes changes through 2026 and forecasts further adaptation without fixed deadlines.
pts.d: The episode is labeled 2026 and places Devlin-Brown's departure from BigLaw in 2025, approximately a year earlier. He dates a substantial change in his own workflow to agentic capabilities arriving around the beginning of the current year. Present benefits depend on hands-on learning, appropriate integration, maintaining case context and human professional judgment. His preferred setup keeps files in a secure enterprise environment. He acknowledges limited memory, temporal confusion and imperfect workflows, and does not generalize his older Harvey demo into a current product evaluation. Future staffing, market and breach predictions have no specific completion dates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern litigation boutiques, large firms, junior and senior lawyers, corporate legal buyers, and legal-AI vendors.
pts.d: Boutiques gain capacity for complex matters and preparation outside their specialty. Partners become more directly involved with smaller teams; juniors lose some tedious work but must develop case knowledge, AI-building skills and judgment. Large firms face uneven adoption, lower leverage and pressure to demonstrate value beyond internally generated client work. In-house departments gain options to internalize tasks and challenge outside costs. Corporate and individual clients may receive more efficient service, but differ in interest in AI itself. Harvey and Legora are discussed as software vendors, not alternative legal service providers. Broader unserved markets are mentioned without identifying beneficiaries or establishing a civil access-to-justice effect.
